topic.subject: science
topic.title: The cell
topic.scope: cell as basic unit, cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, plant vs animal cells, organelles, unicellular vs multicellular

misconceptions.statement: Cells are static like bricks in a wall.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks often use the 'bricks in a wall' analogy for cells, leading to a structural-only view.
misconceptions.fix: Cells are dynamic, living units that perform active metabolic processes, not just passive building blocks.

probe.question: If a cell is like a brick, what happens to it when the organism grows?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays exactly the same size and shape forever.

misconceptions.root_belief: analogies are literal representations of reality

misconceptions.statement: Bigger organisms have bigger cells than smaller organisms.
misconceptions.why: Students intuitively believe that the size of the whole is determined by the size of the parts.
misconceptions.fix: The size of an organism depends on the number of cells, not the size of individual cells.

probe.question: Does an elephant have larger cells than a rat?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the elephant is much bigger.

misconceptions.statement: The cell membrane is a solid, impermeable skin.
misconceptions.why: Diagrams often show a thick line around the cell, suggesting a closed container.
misconceptions.fix: The cell membrane is selectively permeable, allowing specific substances to move in and out.

probe.question: How do nutrients get inside a cell if it has a membrane?
probe.wrong_answer: They wait for the membrane to break or disappear.

misconceptions.statement: The nucleus is the 'brain' of the cell and thinks for it.
misconceptions.why: The common 'brain' analogy leads students to believe the nucleus has consciousness or decision-making power.
misconceptions.fix: The nucleus contains genetic material and coordinates activities through chemical signals, not conscious thought.

probe.question: Does the nucleus 'decide' when to eat?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it thinks and tells the cell what to do.

misconceptions.root_belief: biological parts function like human organs

misconceptions.statement: Only animal cells have mitochondria; plant cells have chloroplasts instead.
misconceptions.why: Students think organelles are mutually exclusive based on the primary energy source.
misconceptions.fix: Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria for cellular respiration; plants just have chloroplasts in addition.

probe.question: Where do plant cells get energy when there is no sunlight?
probe.wrong_answer: They don't need energy at night or they use chloroplasts.

misconceptions.statement: All cells in a plant contain chloroplasts.
misconceptions.fix: Only green parts like leaves have chloroplasts; root cells or internal stem cells usually do not.

probe.question: Would you find chloroplasts in the root cells of an onion?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a plant.

misconceptions.statement: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no DNA because they have no nucleus.
misconceptions.why: Students equate the absence of a container (nucleus) with the absence of the content (DNA).
misconceptions.fix: Prokaryotes have DNA, but it is not enclosed in a nuclear membrane; it lies in the cytoplasm as a nucleoid.

probe.question: How do bacteria pass on traits to their offspring without a nucleus?
probe.wrong_answer: They don't have traits or DNA.

misconceptions.statement: Vacuoles are just empty air bubbles inside the cell.
misconceptions.why: In diagrams, vacuoles are often drawn as empty white spaces.
misconceptions.fix: Vacuoles are fluid-filled sacs containing water, nutrients, or waste products.

probe.question: What is inside a large central vacuole of a plant cell?

misconceptions.statement: Cells are made of atoms, but atoms are not inside cells.
misconceptions.why: Students struggle to bridge the gap between chemistry (atoms) and biology (cells).
misconceptions.fix: Cells are complex structures entirely made of molecules, which are made of atoms.

probe.question: If you zoom into a cell membrane, what would you eventually see?
probe.wrong_answer: Just more cell stuff, not atoms.

misconceptions.statement: The cell wall and cell membrane are the same thing.
misconceptions.why: Both are outer boundaries, and students often use the terms interchangeably.
misconceptions.fix: The cell membrane is a flexible living layer in all cells; the cell wall is a rigid outer layer found only in plants, fungi, and bacteria.

probe.question: Do animal cells have a cell wall?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it's the same as the membrane.

misconceptions.statement: Unicellular organisms are not 'alive' in the same way humans are.
misconceptions.why: Students often associate 'life' with complex organs like hearts or lungs.
misconceptions.fix: A single cell is a complete living organism that performs all essential life processes like respiration and reproduction.

probe.question: Does an Amoeba breathe or eat?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it's too small to have those functions.

misconceptions.statement: The nucleus is the only part of the cell that contains information.
misconceptions.why: Over-emphasis on the nucleus as the 'control center' ignores other organelles.
misconceptions.fix: While the nucleus holds most DNA, mitochondria and chloroplasts also have their own genetic material.

probe.question: Is DNA found anywhere else besides the nucleus?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only the nucleus has DNA.
